title: Math and Bit tricks
summary: GCD, primes, modular power, counting bits

guide.title: Small tricks, huge speed-ups
points: Primes, GCD, modular arithmetic and bit tricks show up in aptitude-style coding rounds and as building blocks inside harder problems.
The right formula replaces a loop of 10¹⁸ steps with one line.
Bit manipulation questions (single number, count set bits, power of two) are quick wins if you know the tricks.

guide.title: Maths and bits in software
points: Online security (HTTPS, UPI, RSA) depends on primes and fast modular power.
Hashing and checksums (CRC, UPI and Aadhaar check digits) use modulo arithmetic.
Feature flags and permissions are stored as bits: read = 1, write = 2, execute = 4; chmod 755 is bits.
Graphics and networking use bit masks: IP subnets (255.255.255.0), RGB colours packed in one integer.

guide.title: Know the core tools
points: GCD by Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), and LCM = a / gcd × b.
Prime check up to √n; many primes at once with the Sieve of Eratosthenes.
Modulo keeps numbers small: (a + b) % m and (a × b) % m can be taken at every step.
Bits: & (and), | (or), ^ (xor), ~ (not), << and >> (shift). x & 1 tells odd or even.

code.python:
from math import gcd
is_odd = lambda x: x & 1 == 1
power_of_two = lambda x: x > 0 and x & (x - 1) == 0
bin(10).count('1')       # set bits: 2

guide.title: Fast power: aⁿ in O(log n)
points: Square the base and halve the exponent; multiply into the result when the current bit of n is 1.
Take % m after every multiplication to keep values small. The answers to "mod 10⁹ + 7" questions rely on this.

code.python:
def power(a, n, m):
    return pow(a, n, m)        # built in, already O(log n)

guide.title: XOR tricks
points: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so XOR-ing a list cancels pairs: the number that appears once is left.
x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit: count set bits by repeating it, or test a power of two.
Subsets as bits: for n items, the numbers 0 .. 2ⁿ − 1 list every subset; bit i says whether item i is taken.

code.javascript:
let single = 0;
for (const x of nums) single ^= x;
code.java:
int single = 0;
for (int x : nums) single ^= x;
code.cpp:
int single = 0;
for (int x : nums) single ^= x;

guide.title: What breaks maths code
points: Overflow: a × b with a, b near 10⁹ needs 64-bit (long / long long) before taking %. JavaScript loses precision past 2⁵³: use BigInt.
Negative modulo: (a − b) % m can be negative in Java, C++ and JavaScript. Add m: ((a − b) % m + m) % m.
Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3. Compare with integers or a small tolerance.
Operator precedence: x & 1 == 1 means x & (1 == 1) in Java, C++ and JavaScript. Use brackets.

guide.title: For advanced learners and interviews
points: Modular inverse with Fermat: a⁻¹ = a^(m − 2) mod m for prime m; used for nCr mod p.
Sieve variants: smallest prime factor sieve factorises many numbers fast.
Bitmask DP solves "visit all cities" style problems for n ≤ 20.
Know Gray code, the inclusion–exclusion principle and the pigeonhole principle for puzzle rounds.
Next step: Lists, Trees and Graphs.

problems.title: Greatest common divisor
problems.statement: Return gcd(a, b) for non-negative integers, not both zero.

problems.title: Prime check
problems.statement: Return true if n is a prime number.
problems.hint: Try divisors up to the square root.

problems.title: Power of two
problems.statement: Return true if n is a power of two.
problems.hint: A power of two has exactly one set bit.

problems.title: Count set bits
problems.statement: Return how many 1 bits the non-negative integer n (below 2^31) has.

problems.title: Single number
problems.statement: Every value appears twice except one. Return that one using O(1) extra space.
inputFormat: nums: integers separated by spaces (may be empty)

problems.title: Count primes below N
problems.statement: Return how many primes are smaller than n (n up to 1,000,000).

problems.title: Modular power
problems.statement: Return (base^exp) % mod. exp can be up to 10^9 and mod up to 10^9+7.
problems.hint: Square and multiply; keep products in 64-bit integers (BigInt in JavaScript) so they stay exact.
